subtopic: Asking parents for something
subtype: Approach: being ready to compromise [Thinking]
passage: During the free period in the school library, Sahil opened his notebook to the page where he'd written CONSOLE, 2000 RUPEES in big letters. His friend Disha peered over. "Your parents said no?" "They said not now. Too much." Sahil tapped his pen. "So I've been thinking. Option one: keep asking and get nothing. Option two: the small handheld one, eight hundred, with old games built in. Option three: wait till my birthday in March, when Nani usually gives a gift." "Which one?" "The handheld has fewer games. March is five months away." He drew a line under option two. "I'd rather have some fun now than none. I can still hope for the big one later." That evening he asked his parents about the handheld, and they said they'd look at it with him on Saturday.

qa.q: What did Sahil write in big letters?
qa.a: CONSOLE, 2000 RUPEES.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel choosing the handheld?
qa.a: A little disappointed not to get the big one, but content and relieved to have a realistic choice.

qa.q: What else could Sahil have considered?
qa.a: Waiting for March and talking it over with his parents then, since a birthday gift might change what is possible.

qa.q: How might Sahil's parents see his new request?
qa.a: They seem pleased by the reasonable compromise, agreeing to look at the handheld with him on Saturday.

grounding: A boy accepts that a cheaper option or waiting for his birthday could work, choosing part of what he wants over nothing.

subtopic: Asking parents for something
subtype: Approach: being ready to compromise [Thinking]
passage: I'm Mridul, Saurabh's cousin. We were at the electronics shop on Sunday, and Saurabh stood in front of the game console for a long time. Two thousand rupees. His father said, "That's a lot for now." I thought Saurabh would sulk. Instead he walked along the shelf, picking things up: a cheaper console with fewer games, a pair of controllers for the old game box at home. Then he came back and said, "Papa, if I get the controllers now, can we think about the console for my birthday?" His father smiled. "That sounds fair." In the car Saurabh was quiet but not sulky. I don't know if he was disappointed. He kept turning the controller box over in his hands.

qa.q: How much did the console cost?
qa.a: Two thousand rupees.

qa.q: What might Saurabh have felt in the car?
qa.a: Perhaps a little disappointed, but also content with getting part of what he wanted.

qa.q: What else could Saurabh have suggested?
qa.a: The cheaper console with fewer games, which would give him a new console now instead of waiting.

qa.q: How does Mridul see Saurabh's choice?
qa.a: Mridul expected sulking and is surprised by the compromise, but cannot tell whether Saurabh was disappointed.

grounding: A cousin watches a boy accept a smaller purchase now and the console perhaps on his birthday, instead of nothing.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: switching to an indoor activity [Revision]
passage: The whole mohalla in their little town had been waiting for Sunday's cricket match against the boys from the station colony. At nine the sky opened. By ten the ground behind the temple was a pond. Swati stood at the door with the bat, her face falling. Her cousin Yogesh kicked the doorframe. "Spoiled. The whole day's spoiled." Swati watched the rain for a minute. Then she turned. "The carrom board is under Dadi's bed. And we have ludo." "Carrom isn't cricket." "No. But all eleven of us are here anyway." By noon, four were playing carrom on the verandah, four were at ludo on the charpai, and the rest were keeping score and shouting. Dadi sent out pakoras. Nobody mentioned cricket until the rain stopped at five.

qa.q: Where was the carrom board?
qa.a: Under Dadi's bed.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel when the match was rained off?
qa.a: Angry and frustrated, kicking the doorframe.

qa.q: What else could the children have done besides indoor games?
qa.a: They could also fix a new date with the station colony boys, so the match is postponed, not lost.

qa.q: How might Dadi see the day?
qa.a: Dadi's house was full of noise and games, and sending out pakoras suggests she enjoyed it.

grounding: When rain cancels a cricket match, the children switch to carrom and ludo and make it a different kind of fun day.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: switching to an indoor activity [Revision]
passage: Javier had planned Saturday's football game at the park for a week. At eleven, thunder rolled over Guadalajara and the rain came down sideways. His little sister Sofia pressed her nose to the window. "No game?" Javier flopped onto the sofa and grumbled for a few minutes. Then he looked at the six friends who had already arrived, dripping, in the hallway. "Okay. New tournament. Indoors." He pulled the old board games out of the cupboard: a racing game with dice, a card game, a wooden board where you flick coins. Sofia wrote a scoreboard on a pizza box. By lunch the flicking game had a champion, Sofia, and everyone was arguing about a rematch. "Best Saturday," one of the boys said, eating a sandwich on the floor.

qa.q: Who became the champion of the flicking game?
qa.a: Sofia.

qa.q: How did Javier feel when he flopped onto the sofa?
qa.a: Disappointed and annoyed that his week-long plan was ruined.

qa.q: What else could Javier have done about the football?
qa.a: Moved it to Sunday or the next dry day, so the game still happens.

qa.q: What was the day like for Sofia?
qa.a: Sofia made the scoreboard and won the flicking game, so it was a great day for her. 🎉

grounding: When rain cancels football, a boy turns the day into an indoor board-game tournament that everyone enjoys.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: thinking of what is still possible [Thinking]
passage: The lights went out across their Penang apartment block at eight, just as Mei was halfway through a video on her tablet. The battery showed 9%. "Useless," she muttered. Then she made herself think. "Okay. What can't I do? Tablet, TV, the fan. What can I do?" She counted on her fingers: there were candles in the kitchen drawer; her book was on the shelf; Grandma knew a hundred stories; and her cousin Yara, staying the night, could sing anything. She lit a candle with Mum, carried it to the living room and announced, "Game. Each person sings a line, and the next song starts with the last word." Grandma began with an old lullaby. By the time the lights came back at ten, nobody had noticed.

qa.q: What did the tablet battery show?
What was Mei feeling when she muttered 'Useless'?
qa.a: Annoyed and frustrated that the power cut interrupted her video.

qa.q: What else could the family do if the cut lasted all night?
qa.a: Read aloud by candlelight or tell Grandma's stories, keeping the tablet charge for emergencies.

qa.q: What was the evening like for Grandma?
qa.a: Grandma got to share an old lullaby with the whole family gathered round.

grounding: During a night power cut, a girl lists what she cannot do and what is still possible, and turns the evening into a singing game.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: thinking of what is still possible [Thinking]
passage: At seven-thirty, in the middle of study hour at the girls' hostel, the power went out, and the whole corridor groaned. Mahima's tablet, with her online worksheet, was at 5%. She switched it off to save the charge. "Okay," she thought. "What can't I do? Worksheet, fan. What can I do?" The emergency lamp in the corridor was glowing. Her poetry book was paper. And eight girls in one dorm meant a lot of songs. She went to the warden, Rukmini-ma'am, and asked if they could sit under the emergency lamp. First they read the poems for tomorrow's test aloud, taking turns. Then someone started antakshari. When the lights came on at nine, Rukmini-ma'am said theirs had been the calmest dorm, apart from the singing.

qa.q: When did the power go out?
qa.a: At seven-thirty, during study hour.

qa.q: What was Mahima thinking when she switched off the tablet?
qa.a: A little disappointed, but calm and practical, working out what was still possible.

qa.q: What else could Mahima do about the online worksheet?
qa.a: Tell her teacher in the morning about the cut, and finish it once the tablet is charged.

qa.q: How did Rukmini-ma'am see the evening?
qa.a: Rukmini-ma'am was pleased that theirs was the calmest dorm, apart from the singing.

grounding: During a hostel power cut, a girl thinks about what is still possible and leads reading and antakshari under the emergency lamp.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: sulking and blaming [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Vandana, Jatin's aunt, and I'd come over for the picnic that never happened. When the rain started at nine, Jatin threw himself on the sofa and said, "Everything's spoiled. Everything." His mother spread the picnic sheet on the living-room floor and set out the aloo sandwiches. Jatin didn't move. His father put on the old songs and started a card game with the little ones. Jatin said, "This isn't a picnic." We made chai and hot pakoras, and everyone sat on the sheet laughing when the baby tried to eat a card. Jatin stayed on the sofa with his arms folded all afternoon. In the evening he asked if there were any pakoras left. There weren't. I don't know if he was angry at the rain or at us.

qa.q: What did Jatin's mother spread on the floor?
qa.a: The picnic sheet.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling on the sofa?
qa.a: Angry and disappointed that the picnic was spoiled.

qa.q: How does Vandana see Jatin's afternoon?
qa.a: Vandana sees him miss the fun and the pakoras, but doesn't know whether he was angry at the rain or at the family.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: preparing a torch and candles in advance [Action]
passage: Every summer in our town, the lights go off at least twice a week, usually just when Dadi is cooking. Last year I got tired of everyone stumbling around shouting, "Where's the torch?" So I, Pradeep, took an old biscuit tin and put in the big torch, a box of matches for the grown-ups, two candles and Dadi's palm-leaf hand fan. I kept it on the shelf right next to the kitchen door, and I told everyone, even my little cousin Mahima. The next time the power went, I walked straight to the shelf in the dark, three steps from the door. In ten seconds the torch was on and Dadi had her fan. She said I was the family's electricity board. Now I check the torch batteries every Sunday.

qa.q: What did Pradeep put in the tin?
qa.a: The big torch, a box of matches for the grown-ups, two candles and Dadi's palm-leaf hand fan.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel when Dadi called it the family's electricity board?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud and pleased that the plan worked.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep add to the tin?
qa.a: Spare torch batteries, so a flat battery doesn't undo the whole plan.

qa.q: What is the next power cut like for Dadi?
qa.a: Dadi gets light and her fan in ten seconds instead of waiting in the dark.

grounding: Looking back, a child describes keeping a torch, matches and a hand fan in a known place for summer power cuts.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: preparing a torch and candles in advance [Action]
passage:
Class 4 note, April.
After last week's power cut, when our room went dark during the drawing period and three children panicked, Madhav came to me with an idea. "Can we keep a torch in class? And the paper fans we made?" We agreed a plan together. He brought a shoebox, labelled it POWER CUT in big letters, and packed two torches from the office, the paper fans and a whistle for the class monitor. He chose the spot himself: the first shelf by the door, "so anyone can find it without looking". Today the lights went out again at noon. Before I could speak, Madhav had the torches on and was handing out fans. The class stayed calm. I have asked him to check the torch batteries every Monday.
Mehak, class teacher

qa.q: Where did Madhav keep the box?
qa.a: On the first shelf by the door.

qa.q: How did Madhav likely feel when the lights went out today?
qa.a: Calm and ready, and probably proud as he handed out the fans.

qa.q: What else could help the class in future cuts?
qa.a: A short practice, so every child knows where the box is and what to do.

qa.q: How did the class experience today's power cut?
qa.a: The class stayed calm, with torches and fans ready in moments.

grounding: A teacher's note records a child preparing a power-cut box in a known place and helping the class quickly when the lights go out.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: making a back-up plan for outdoor events [Thinking]
passage: Parveen, you're worried about the clouds for your party? Let me tell you about your Ammi. When Kiran was ten, she wanted her birthday in our back garden, under the mango tree. The day before, the radio said, "Chance of showers." Everyone said, "We'll see." Kiran said, "No. If we see tomorrow, it'll be too late." She sat on the step and thought it through out loud. "If it rains, we go into the big hall. Musical chairs works in the hall. The treasure hunt works too, if I hide things behind cushions instead of bushes. Only the sack race needs the garden." So she made two lists of hiding places. At four o'clock it poured. Twenty children ran inside, and the treasure hunt began in the hall as if it had always been planned there.

qa.q: What did the radio say the day before?
qa.a: "Chance of showers."

qa.q: What was Kiran thinking on the step?
qa.a: She was worried rain could spoil the party, but determined, working out which games could move indoors.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the party work?
qa.a: Making two lists of hiding places and checking which games worked in the hall, before the rain came.

qa.q: How might the twenty children have experienced the rain?
qa.a: They simply ran inside and carried on with the treasure hunt, so the party was not spoiled.

grounding: An elder recalls a girl planning a garden birthday with a ready indoor plan and games that worked in both places.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: making a back-up plan for outdoor events [Thinking]
passage: Kavitha's party was on the terrace at five, and at two the sky over their Chennai building turned grey. Worse, the building secretary, who kept the key to the ground-floor hall, was away at a wedding. Kavitha thought fast. "If it rains, we need a roof. The hall is locked. What else has a roof?" Their own flat was too small for fifteen. Then she remembered that Noor's family on the first floor had a big covered balcony. She ran down, and Noor's mother said yes. Kavitha split her games into two piles: pass the parcel and dumb charades worked anywhere; the water-balloon game only on the terrace. At half past four it poured. Everyone trooped to Noor's balcony, and the parcel went round to the sound of rain.

qa.q: Who kept the key to the hall?
qa.a: The building secretary.

qa.q: How did Kavitha feel when the sky turned grey?
qa.a: Anxious, but she kept thinking quickly about where else had a roof.

qa.q: What else could Kavitha have done differently?
qa.a: Planned the back-up a day earlier, before the key holder left, so there were more choices.

qa.a: Noor's family hosted unexpectedly, with their covered balcony suddenly full of children.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: finishing homework before the battery dies [Action]
passage: Last July our class had an online science quiz due on Friday night. I'm Jomon. On Wednesday evening the weather bulletin said a big storm would reach our district on Thursday. I remembered the last storm: no power for a whole day and no internet for two. My friend Divyansh said, "There's still Friday." But I thought, what if there isn't? So on Wednesday night I did the quiz, all twenty questions, and submitted it. Then I printed the notes for the next chapter at the shop downstairs, in case the lights went. The storm came on Thursday afternoon. The power was off till Saturday. On Monday half the class had missed the quiz. Mine was already marked.

qa.q: When was the quiz due?
qa.a: On Friday night.

qa.q: How did Jomon likely feel on Monday?
qa.a: Relieved, and probably proud of having finished before the storm.

qa.q: What else could Jomon do when a storm is forecast?
qa.a: Charge devices early and tell the teacher in advance if work might not reach on time.

qa.q: What would change if Jomon had waited for Friday, as Divyansh suggested?
qa.a: With the power off until Saturday, Jomon would likely have missed the quiz like half the class.

grounding: Looking back, a child hears a storm forecast, finishes online work early and prints notes so an outage cannot block the deadline.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans

passage:
Class 6 teacher's note, after the cyclone warning.
On Tuesday the weather office warned that a cyclone would reach our coast on Thursday. The class project was due online on Friday. On Wednesday morning Zubin came to me with a printed copy of his project and a question: "I've uploaded it already. Can I also give you this, in case the internet goes?" He had finished it on Tuesday night, three days early, and printed his revision notes at the stationery shop too. The cyclone cut power to most of the town for two days. On Monday, eleven students asked for extensions. Zubin's work was already marked. I have shared his idea with the class: when a storm is forecast, finish early and keep a paper copy.
Minakshi, class teacher

qa.a: Eleven.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: safety thinking during a storm [Thinking]
passage: The storm hit their Mumbai flat at six in the evening. Thunder shook the windows and the lights flickered. Noor's little brother Varun ran to the window to watch the lightning. Noor's heart thumped, but she made herself remember the safety talk from school. "Away from windows," she said, pulling Varun back to the sofa in the middle of the room. "Unplug the TV." She switched it off at the wall first, then pulled the plug with dry hands. Water was dripping near the balcony switchboard. "Don't touch that. Wet switches are dangerous." Outside, a cable swung loose from the pole. "And if we go out, we keep away from wires." When their mother came home soaked at eight, the two of them were in the middle of the room, playing cards by torchlight.

qa.q: Where did Noor pull Varun to?
qa.a: To the sofa in the middle of the room.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when the storm hit?
qa.a: Scared, with her heart thumping, but she steadied herself by remembering the rules.

qa.q: What else could Noor do if something sparked or the water spread?
qa.a: Keep Varun well away and call their mother or a neighbour straight away.

qa.q: How might their mother feel coming home?
qa.a: Relieved to find both children safe in the middle of the room.

grounding: During a storm, a girl recalls school safety rules: away from windows, unplug the TV, avoid wet switches and loose wires.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: safety thinking during a storm [Thinking]
passage:
"Leela, let's charge the phone, the battery's low!"
"Not now, Avni. There's lightning. We unplug things, we don't plug them in."
"Who says?"
"Our science teacher. Remember the safety talk? Unplug the TV, stay away from windows."
"But the window's the best view!"
"The best view of getting hurt. Come to the middle of the room."
"Fine. What about the fan switch? It's hot."
"Your hands are wet from the rain. Just leave the switches."
"You're so careful."
"And if the lane floods, we don't walk near the electric pole. There was a loose wire last year."
"Okay, okay. So what do we do?"
"Snakes and ladders. On the floor. In the middle."
A crack of thunder. Avni scooted closer. "Middle of the floor it is."

qa.q: What did Avni want to charge?
qa.a: The phone.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling while listing the rules?
qa.a: Serious and a little worried, wanting them both to stay safe.

qa.q: What else could Leela do if the power goes out?
qa.a: Use a torch rather than touching switches, and tell an adult if anything sparks.

qa.q: How does Avni's view of the rules change?
qa.a: Avni first calls Leela 'so careful', but after the thunder moves to the middle of the floor.

grounding: During a storm, a child remembers school safety rules about switches, windows and wires and keeps a friend safe.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
subtype: Approach: turning the problem into a game [Revision]
passage: The power in their Kolkata lane went at six, and the electricity office said it would be back "late night". Arnab, lying on the floor, pointed the torch at the ceiling and saw his hand throw a huge shadow. He curled two fingers. A dog's head appeared on the wall. Raghav stopped sulking. "Do a crocodile." Within half an hour they had hung a white bedsheet from the cupboard and were making up a story about a dog who stole a crocodile's lunch. Their grandmother came to watch with her tea. When the lights came back at eleven, Raghav groaned. "Already?"

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans

passage:
"Didi, I'm bored. When is the light coming?"
"Nobody knows, Sachin. Maybe ten."
"It's only seven! I can't read, I can't watch anything, it's hot..."
"You've said 'hot' eleven times."
"Because it's hot!"
Nandini sighed and switched on the torch. The beam hit the wall. She hooked her thumbs together and flapped her fingers. "Look."
"A bird!"
"A crow. And the crow is very hungry." She made its beak open and shut. "Caw. Where is Sachin's dinner?"
Sachin giggled. "Let me do one!" He made a lumpy shape. "It's a... rabbit?"
"It's a potato with ears."
"The potato is scared of the crow!"
By the time Amma called them for dinner, the crow and the potato were best friends and had fought off a cat.

subtopic: A power cut or rain spoils plans
